Your Rights When The Cops Pull You Over Explained In One Brilliant Infographic

Thank you for posting this. While it isn't fully comprehensive by virtue of being a quick infographic, it does address some of the things I see frequently when police are vilified in the media. No doubt the most public scrutiny develops around the most egregious offenses of police malpractice, but the fact is that many of the victims of police brutality escalate the situation by behaving inappropriately. This is not to blame the victim, but rather to state that the most effective way to fight police corruption and brutality is through faithful documentation, polite interaction (as well as can be managed), and court action after the fact.

To speak of a specific example, there is almost certainly some shady shit happening with the Bland case outside of Houston, TX, but one thing that irked me about the footage released was her insistence that she could not be arrested for the offense committed (not signalling a lane change was cited by the officer). This is, to my knowledge, false (although IANAL). The only driving offenses for which police cannot arrest a suspect in Texas are speeding (but the officer may assess that significant speeding may warrant a reckless driving citation, which is arrestable) and open container (for which they can be arrested under suspicion of DWI or DUI until a breathalyzer or blood test). The officer severely bungled the situation in that his conduct clearly escalated the interaction unduly. However, her actual arrest was completely legal, and I feel it was largely and regretfully avoidable.

Therefore, kudos to OP and anyone who disseminates accurate and useful information for interaction with the police. Legal precedent has given an advantage to police power, but ignorance cannot help one defend what rights he or she does have. In short, don't be this guy, who I would have arrested for at least three things were I police: refusal to identify himself by name when asked (Hiibel v. Sixth Judicial District Court of Nevada), a reasonable implication of terrorist threat when he went on about "the eighth is the day of rage" and didn't clarify what it meant when asked, and (to a lesser extent) his repeated insistence that if "you mess with me any further, I will shoot [to] kill [to] protect myself." While it is certainly legal to shoot and even kill a police officer in Texas should he or she violate the rights of the accused in manner for which deadly force is protected, simple presence outside of a vehicle is not such a situation. While the interior of vehicles are granted certain constitutional protections from search and seizure, the exterior is more in the realm of "I'm not touching you" territory. Plus the dude was a certifiable asshole, so I personally would have been angling for a way to arrest him. Perhaps it's better that I'm not police.
